name: Mojo
year_note: Work on the compiler began at Modular in 2022 (its first patch, a lexer, landed on 27 September 2022). Mojo was announced on 2 May 2023 with a hosted Playground; a local SDK followed for Linux on 7 September 2023 (v0.2.1) and for macOS on 19 October 2023. Mojo 1.0 was released on 11 August 2026.
tagline: Python syntax over an MLIR-based systems core: compile-time parameters, SIMD types and ownership for CPUs, GPUs and accelerators.
summary: Mojo is a statically typed, compiled systems programming language from Modular that adopts Python's syntax while taking its semantics from Rust, Swift and C++: value-semantic structs, traits, and ownership expressed through argument conventions. Its centrepiece is a compile-time parameter system (square-bracket parameters, code evaluated by the compiler with `comptime`, and SIMD vector types beneath every number) used to write portable high-performance kernels for CPUs, GPUs and other accelerators. It is built directly on the MLIR compiler framework and interoperates with CPython in both directions.
history:
Chris Lattner, who created LLVM, Clang and Swift and started MLIR at Google, co-founded Modular with Tim Davis in 2022 to build AI infrastructure; at Google he had also led Swift for TensorFlow, an unsuccessful attempt to make Swift a replacement for Python in machine learning. Mojo grew out of the need to write the kernels behind Modular's inference engine (MAX) for many kinds of hardware: the first compiler patch landed in September 2022, and by late 2022 a prototype of its parameter system produced matrix-multiplication code matching vendor BLAS libraries on a range of CPUs. Modular announced Mojo on 2 May 2023 with a browser-based Playground and described its long-term goal as becoming a superset of Python, citing the team's experience of moving Objective-C code to Swift; Jeremy Howard of fast.ai called it "syntax sugar for MLIR", as Swift was for LLVM.

The language changed quickly and often incompatibly. `let` was removed in 2024, the standard library was open-sourced under Apache 2.0 in March 2024, and the argument conventions went from `borrowed`/`inout`/`owned` to `read`/`mut`/`var` (2024–25) and, in 1.0, `imm`. Version 25.4 (June 2025) added Python-style comprehensions, AMD GPU support and calls from Python into Mojo; 26.2 (March 2026) made `def` the standard function keyword, with the stricter semantics of the deprecated `fn`, and replaced `@parameter if`/`for` with `comptime if`/`for`. Classes, dynamic typing and full Python compatibility were deferred to a later roadmap phase, which now says Mojo "may or may not evolve into a full superset of Python".

Mojo 1.0 shipped on 11 August 2026 with semantic versioning and stability guarantees for the core language, and on 18 August the compiler and tooling were open-sourced under the Apache 2.0 licence with LLVM exceptions. Qualcomm had agreed to acquire Modular in June 2026. Mojo 1.1 (September 2026) removed the last legacy spellings (`fn`, `alias`, `@parameter if`/`for`).
innovations: Built on MLIR rather than directly on LLVM, so one language targets CPUs, GPUs and other accelerators and can express MLIR operations itself ('syntax sugar for MLIR')

A unified compile-time parameter system: square-bracket type and value parameters, ordinary functions run by an in-compiler interpreter (`comptime`), `comptime if`/`for`, and `where` constraints checked before instantiation
SIMD[dtype, width] as the foundation of the numeric types: every scalar, Int included, is a one-lane SIMD vector
Python syntax (def, indentation, comprehensions, dunder methods) on top of Rust-style ownership expressed through named argument conventions (imm, mut, var, out, deinit) and the ^ transfer sigil
As-soon-as-possible destruction: values are destroyed right after their last use rather than at the end of their scope
Two-way interoperability with CPython: import Python modules into Mojo, and export Mojo functions and types as Python extension modules

typing.notes: Argument and return types must be annotated; `var` declarations infer theirs from the initializer. Trait conformance is declared, never structural. Numeric types are fixed-width and are not converted implicitly (Int is Scalar[DType.int]). Values reached through Python interop are PythonObjects, typed dynamically by CPython.

memory_note: Every value has one owner and is destroyed as soon as possible after its last use; a lifetime checker tracks references (origins) and enforces exclusive mutable access. There is no garbage collector or implicit reference counting: ArcPointer gives opt-in shared ownership, and Pointer with alloc()/dealloc() gives manual control.

influenced_by.note: Syntax (def, indentation, comprehensions, dunder methods, exceptions), naming and CPython interop. Mojo was announced as aiming to become a Python superset; it is not source-compatible, and the roadmap now calls a full superset optional.

Same designer (Chris Lattner), and named in both the 2023 'Why Mojo' document and the current vision among the languages Mojo draws on. Like Swift it is built around value-semantic structs, started with `inout` argument conventions (now `mut`), and plays the part for MLIR that Swift, 'syntax sugar for LLVM', played for LLVM.
Ownership, borrow-checked references and lifetimes (origins), traits with default methods, and naming conventions; named in the vision document and the manual.
The parameter system is described as taking 'the ideas behind C++ templates (compile-time polymorphism and specialization)'; comptime evaluation is likened to constexpr.
Named in the vision document as a source for metaprogramming; Mojo adopted the same `comptime` keyword in 2025.
Listed in Wikipedia's infobox; Mojo calls C through an FFI and exports C-ABI functions (abi("C")).
Named, with Rust, Swift, Zig and Nim, among the languages whose lessons Mojo benefits from in the 2023 'Why Mojo' document.

influenced_by_external.name: MLIR
influenced_by_external.note: The compiler infrastructure Lattner started at Google; Mojo's KGEN compiler is built on MLIR Core and can express MLIR operations directly.

influenced_by_external.name: CUDA
influenced_by_external.note: The vision document cites kernel programming systems (CUDA, CUTLASS) as inspiration for Mojo's kernel-writing model.

influenced_by_external.name: Cython
influenced_by_external.note: The 2023 'Why Mojo' document compares Mojo with earlier Python supersets, Pyrex and Cython; Wikipedia lists Cython as an influence.

structured-control.note: Python-style if/elif/else, while and for…in; `comptime if` and `comptime for` select or unroll code at compile time.

block-scope.note: Every variable is declared with `var` and scoped to its block, unlike Python's function scope; implicit declaration by assignment became an error in 1.1.

exceptions.note: `raises`, raise and try/except/else/finally, compiled as alternate return values rather than stack unwinding (so they also work in GPU kernels); typed errors (`raises MyError`) since 26.1. Functions are non-raising unless declared `raises`.

generators.note: Python-style iterator protocol (__iter__/__next__) behind for…in, plus iter and itertools; there is no `yield`.

type-inference.note: Local: `var` bindings, parameters inferred from arguments and `Some[Trait]`; function signatures are explicit.

generics.note: Square-bracket parameters take types and compile-time values (List[T], SIMD[dtype, width], Array[T, n]) and are specialised per instantiation, with trait bounds, `where` clauses and conditional conformance.

algebraic-data-types.note: Variant[A, B, …] in std.utils is a tagged union, tested with isa[T]() and read with v[T]; native enums and pattern matching are on the roadmap.

type-classes.note: Traits constrain parameterized code and are resolved at compile time, with default methods, required comptime members and conditional conformance; conformance is declared on the struct itself (no retroactive conformance).

option-types.note: Optional[T] from the standard library prelude; ordinary values and references cannot be null.

gradual-typing.note: Only at the Python boundary: PythonObject values are dispatched dynamically through CPython inside statically typed code. Untyped Python-style Mojo code is a future roadmap phase.

ownership.note: One owner per value; arguments are immutable references by default (`imm`), `mut` for mutable references and `var` to take ownership, with `^` transferring a value and ending its variable's lifetime. A lifetime checker tracks origins and forbids aliasing a `mut` argument.

interfaces.note: Traits, conformed to explicitly; dispatch is static, since dynamic trait objects (existentials) are not yet available.

traits-mixins.note: Default method implementations in traits are mixed into every conforming struct; conflicting defaults must be resolved by hand.

abstract-data-types.note: Structs bundle fields and methods, but there is no access control yet: privacy is an underscore convention, and `private` members are a roadmap item.

modules.note: Every .mojo file is a module; a directory with __init__.mojo is a package, which can be precompiled to a .mojoc file.

operator-overloading.note: Python-style dunder methods (__add__, __eq__, __getitem__ and their reversed and in-place forms) on structs.

first-class-functions.note: Functions are values with `def(...) -> T` types; `lambda` expressions since 1.0 (2026).

closures.note: Nested functions and lambdas capture outer values through an explicit capture list, e.g. `{imm x, mut y, var z^}`, which fixes whether each is read, mutated, copied or moved. These unified closures (1.0 beta, 2026) replaced the older @parameter-decorated closures.

list-comprehensions.note: Python-style list, dict and set comprehensions.

immutability.note: Arguments are immutable by default (`imm`), but variables are mutable; there are no immutable run-time bindings since `let` was removed in 2024 (`comptime` names are compile-time constants).

lazy-evaluation.note: Evaluation is strict; std.iter and std.itertools provide lazy iterator adapters.

reference-counting.note: ArcPointer, an atomically reference-counted pointer in std.memory, for opt-in shared ownership.

pointers.note: Pointer[T, origin] (unified with UnsafePointer in 1.0) carries its origin for the lifetime checker, with unsafety marked on individual operations such as unsafe_write(); alloc() and dealloc() manage heap memory. Used mainly for FFI and data structures.

async-await.note: `async def` and `await` exist and compile to coroutines, but the model is unfinished: the public coroutine and task APIs were made private in 1.1, and first-class async is a roadmap item.

reflection.note: Compile-time only: reflect[T] exposes a struct's name, fields and field types to parameterized code; dynamic reflection is planned.

compile-time-execution.note: The compiler interprets ordinary Mojo functions to compute `comptime` values and parameters, including heap-allocating code; `comptime for` unrolls loops and `comptime if` removes dead branches.

array-programming.note: SIMD[dtype, width] vectors apply arithmetic elementwise with reductions, and std.algorithm provides vectorize and map; tensors and layouts come from the MAX libraries.

significant-whitespace.note: Python's off-side rule: a colon and indentation delimit blocks.

milestones.event: First Mojo compiler patch, a lexer (27 September); a parameter-system prototype matches vendor BLAS on CPU matrix multiplication
Announced at Modular's launch with a hosted Mojo Playground (2 May)
First local SDK, v0.2.1 for Linux (7 September); macOS follows in October
Standard library open-sourced under Apache 2.0 (v24.2, March)
v24.6: `inout` and `borrowed` become `mut` and `read`; new `out` convention
v25.4: comprehensions, AMD GPU support and calling Mojo from Python
v26.2: `def` replaces `fn` as the single function keyword; `comptime if` and `comptime for`
Mojo 1.0 (11 August); compiler open-sourced under Apache 2.0 with LLVM exceptions (18 August)
Mojo 1.1 removes the legacy `fn`, `alias` and `@parameter if`/`for` spellings (17 September)

trivia: In the week of its first compiler patch (September 2022) the team chose square brackets rather than angle brackets for generics, for consistency with Python and to avoid the less-than ambiguity.
Until version 26.2 (March 2026) Mojo source files could use the fire emoji as their extension (hello.🔥), and package files the package emoji (📦).
Modular's FAQ explains the name: mojo means 'a magical charm' or 'magical powers'.

hello.notes: Every program needs a `main()` entry point: unlike Python, a .mojo file cannot contain top-level statements. `def` has been Mojo's only function keyword since 26.2; earlier code often used `fn`.

factorial.notes: Argument and return types are required. Int is a fixed-width 64-bit machine integer (an alias for Scalar[DType.int]), not Python's arbitrary-precision int: factorial(21) silently wraps to a negative number.

fizzbuzz.notes: Reads exactly like Python, but it is compiled ahead of time to native code, and `i` is a statically typed Int.

higher-order.notes: A Python-style list comprehension (supported since 25.4) builds a List[Int], and String.join takes any list (as a Span) of Writable values. Lambdas exist since 1.0 (`lambda (x: Int) -> Int: x * x`), but comprehensions are the idiomatic form, as in Python.

shapes.notes: Structs declare their traits explicitly, and @fieldwise_init generates the constructor. `Some[Shape]` is shorthand for a compile-time type parameter `[S: Shape]`, so describe() is specialised for each struct (static dispatch). Mojo has no classes, inheritance or dynamic trait objects yet; a mixed list of shapes would need Variant[Rectangle, Triangle].

signature.title: Compile-time parameters and SIMD
signature.notes: Square brackets hold parameters, which the compiler must know; parentheses hold run-time arguments. `dot` infers its element type and width (the `//` marks infer-only parameters), so the same source is compiled once for 4 x float32 and once for 8 x int16. `comptime for` unrolls power[3]() into three vector multiplies, and fib(20) runs inside the compiler's interpreter, so the program only prints a constant. Older code spells these `alias F = fib(20)` (before 25.7) and `@parameter for` (before 26.2); both spellings were removed in 1.1.

toolchains.name: Mojo (mojo-compiler, PyPI)
toolchains.notes: plw-mojo is python:3.14-slim (Debian 13) with the mojo-compiler 1.1.0 wheel from PyPI (the compiler and standard library, without the LSP and debugger of the full `mojo` package) and gcc, which Mojo uses as its linker driver on Linux. Telemetry is disabled (MODULAR_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false) and HOME=/tmp keeps the compile cache in the tmpfs. In the sandbox (2 CPUs) `mojo build` takes about 1.7–2.2 s per snippet at under 200 MB of memory, and the binaries run in milliseconds; `mojo run {file}` compiles and runs in one step in about the same time. It also works with a read-only root filesystem as a non-root user. The compiler requires an x86-64-v3 (AVX2) or ARM64 host CPU.

runtime.notes: The compiler targets native code and GPUs and does not run in the browser. Modular's 2023 Mojo Playground compiled code on hosted JupyterHub servers.
